description: Developing body literacy and mastering somatic regulation techniques to maintain autonomic equilibrium within the resilient zone.

objectives.objective_title: Identify and name physical body sensations associated with various emotional states.

learning_content.title: Understanding Body Sensations
learning_content.content: Body literacy involves noticing, interpreting, and naming physical sensations...

activities.title: Match each sensation to its likely category
activities.instructions: Drag each sensation into Pleasant, Neutral, or Unpleasant. There may be more than one reasonable answer—this activity is about noticing your own experience.
sensations: Steady pressure where your feet touch the floor
activities.reflection: Did any sensation feel different from what you expected?

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of tracking?
questions.explanation: Tracking involves noticing and categorizing bodily sensations without judgment.

reflection.question: What physical sensations do you notice when you experience stress?

objectives.objective_title: Define the resilient zone and recognize signs of hyper-arousal and hypo-arousal dysregulation.

activities.title: What Would You Do?
activities.instructions: Read the situation and choose the response that shows the most empathy.
activities.scenario: Your friend is sitting alone and looks upset. When you ask if everything is okay, they say, 'I don't want to talk about it.'

options.text: You should tell me what's wrong.
Okay. If you ever feel like talking, I'm here for you.
You shouldn't be upset about it.

feedback.correct: Good choice! You respected your friend's feelings and gave them space while showing that you are available to support them.
feedback.A: Not quite. Asking someone to explain themselves can make them feel pressured. Try giving them space while letting them know you are available.
feedback.C: Not quite. Telling someone how they should feel can dismiss their emotions. Try acknowledging their feelings instead.

reflection.question: What signs might indicate that you are outside your resilient zone?

objectives.objective_title: Distinguish between the alerting functions of the sympathetic nervous system and the calming functions of the parasympathetic nervous system.

reflection.question: How can understanding your body's nervous-system responses help you respond to stress?

objectives.objective_title: Apply tracking, grounding, and resourcing techniques to restore emotional balance during stress.

activities.title: Contact Grounding Practice
steps: Select a comfortable seated or standing position.
Direct attention to points of contact between your body and supportive objects.
Rest focus on neutral or pleasant sensations.

reflection.question: Which grounding or resourcing technique feels most useful to you?

definitions.definition: The ability to perceive, interpret, and name physical body sensations to understand underlying emotional states.
A state of nervous system equilibrium where an individual can process emotions effectively and make clear decisions under stress.
A state where stress pushes the autonomic nervous system out of balance, resulting in hyper-arousal (stuck on high) or hypo-arousal (stuck on low).
The branch of the autonomic nervous system responsible for activating the fight, flight, or freeze threat-response mechanism.
The branch of the autonomic nervous system that mediates relaxation, recovery, and bodily restoration.
Intentionally observing present physical sensations and labeling them as pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral.
Directing attention to the physical contact between the body and a supportive external surface to foster stability.
Vividly recalling a sensory-rich positive memory, person, or place to induce calming physiological states.

examples.scenario: A student experiences cold hands and shallow breathing before speaking publicly. They press their feet firmly into the floor to ground their body and stabilize their voice.
A driver encounters sudden vehicle trouble on the highway. Noticing a racing pulse and tight chest, they recognize early dysregulation before shouting at surrounding motorists.
An examinee feels overwhelmed during a test and visualizes a calm mountain retreat to activate parasympathetic relaxation and recover focus.

instructions: Observe present bodily sensations without attempting to change or judge them.
Categorize observed sensations using descriptive sensation words rather than emotional labels.
Establish physical grounding by bringing awareness to solid points of contact when feeling dysregulated.
Engage all five senses when summoning a mental resource to maximize physiological calming.
reflection: How do your physical body sensations shift when transitioning from a stressful thought to a grounded state?
Which specific sensory anchor provides you with the most rapid sense of physical stability?

definitions.definition: The ability to maintain core values and personal integrity while speaking and acting under stress or external pressure.
A state of active caution and restraint regarding thoughts, speech, or actions that could cause harm to self or others.
Intentionally holding core values and positive behaviors in working memory to guide present conduct.
Real-time consciousness of one's immediate speech, actions, and mental states in the present moment.
The capacity to maintain continuous focus on a chosen object or task without distraction.
The ability to monitor mental processes and recognize when attention has drifted from its intended focus.

Facing time pressure during an examination, a student applies ethical mindfulness to maintain honesty rather than resorting to unethical shortcuts.

instructions: Identify potential psychological hazards or impulsive habits before entering challenging situations.
Keep core ethical principles actively present in mind when communicating under stress.
Monitor ongoing verbal and physical conduct in real time to prevent accidental harm.

definitions.definition: The continuous monitoring of internal psychological states to differentiate constructive emotions from destructive impulses.
Attitudes and emotional orientations (e.g., gratitude, generosity) that promote personal well-being and social harmony.
Psychological conditions (e.g., resentment, envy, anger) that distort reality and generate suffering for oneself and others.
A framework illustrating how a minor emotional precondition escalates through triggers into destructive behavioral outbursts.
The intentional intervention during emotional arousal where an individual chooses constructive responses over automatic reactions.

examples.scenario: A student running late spills tea on their attire. Recognizing the trigger prevents anger from escalating into an all-day hostile mood toward family members.
A professional notices rising frustration during a heated debate and applies a brief pause to prevent an aggressive verbal conflict.

instructions: Observe mental states as temporary psychological events rather than permanent aspects of identity.
Classify emerging emotions as either beneficial or harmful based on their long-term outcomes.
Identify early physical and cognitive indicators of emotional escalation.
Utilize grounding techniques during the selective filtering window to choose value-aligned responses.

definitions.definition: Recognizing one's intrinsic value, treating oneself with understanding during setbacks, and actively supporting one's genuine well-being.
The cognitive trap of perpetually pursuing external accomplishments or possessions without ever attaining lasting satisfaction.
Rigid, perfectionist standards that distort self-assessment and generate perpetual disappointment.
The cognitive tendency to overestimate one's abilities, status, or correctness relative to others.
The habitual underestimation of one's intrinsic worth and capabilities leading to avoidance or burnout.
The insistence on flawlessness and severe self-judgment in response to minor errors.
Four dualities of external attachment and aversion: Financial Gain vs. Loss, Pleasure vs. Pain, Praise vs. Blame, and Status vs. Insignificance.

examples.scenario: An applicant passed over for a promotion refrains from harsh self-condemnation, evaluating areas for growth while maintaining self-worth.
An individual recognizes that purchasing a new flagship smartphone provides only temporary pleasure, stepping off the hedonic treadmill.

instructions: Acknowledge intrinsic human worth regardless of recent performance or external status.
Differentiate between constructive goals (aspirations) and rigid conditions for self-worth (expectations).
Identify attachment to external praise, financial gain, or status as temporary conditions.
Adopt an encouraging, non-judgmental internal voice during moments of failure or distress.

The practice of reducing group-based favoritism and extending compassionate consideration to all human beings.
The systematic tendency to favor members of one's own social, cultural, or demographic group over outsiders.
The inclination to view individuals outside one's immediate group with indifference, distrust, or hostility.
A standardized, oversimplified mental picture attributed to an entire group of people.
A preconceived, ungrounded negative attitude directed toward an individual based on group identity.
The false belief that social categories possess fixed, immutable characteristics that define a person's entire nature.

activities.title: Three Levels of Compassion Mapping
steps: Select a major issue or suffering currently observed in your community.
Formulate a Wishing Compassion statement reflecting passive hope.
Formulate an Aspiring Compassion plan involving indirect or small-scale support.
Formulate an Engaged Compassion strategy detailing direct, hands-on action.

questions.explanation: Engaged compassion is characterized by direct personal responsibility and active measures to alleviate suffering.

reflection.question: In what areas of your life do you remain stuck in 'wishing compassion' rather than advancing to 'aspiring' or 'engaged' action?

questions.answer: Noticing Suffering, Empathic Concern, Sense of Agency
questions.explanation: Compassion requires perceiving distress (noticing), valuing the sufferer (empathic concern), and possessing confidence to act (sense of agency).

definitions.definition: The active motivation to relieve the suffering of others, rooted in genuine care, critical inquiry, and self-confidence.
The perceptive capacity to recognize visible pain as well as subtle, unseen emotional distress in others.
The internal confidence and belief that one's personal actions can produce meaningful relief.
The passive desire for others to be free from suffering without taking personal responsibility or action.
The active intention to reduce suffering accompanied by preliminary or indirect personal efforts.
Direct, committed, and sustained personal action taken to relieve suffering and address its root causes.

examples.scenario: Hearing of a flood, an individual progresses from hoping victims find safety (wishing) to sending supplies (aspiring) to traveling to the site to assist in cleanup (engaged).
Noticing a quiet colleague struggling with a project, a coworker offers specific task assistance while maintaining respectful boundaries.

instructions: Cultivate active awareness to detect subtle, non-verbal indicators of distress in peers.
Reinforce your sense of agency by focusing on manageable, high-impact actions.
Combine compassionate motivation with critical inquiry to ensure actions address root causes effectively.
Balance engaged compassion toward external causes with foundational self-compassion to maintain well-being.
